<div style="max-width:46rem; margin-top:1.5rem;">
  <div class="kicker">Economist · Applied Microeconomics</div>
  <h1 style="font-size:2.7rem; margin-bottom:1rem;">Sam Absher</h1>
  <p class="lede">
    I study what policies actually do to the people they touch — border
    enforcement, regime change, revolutions, school quality — using the tools of
    causal inference: synthetic control, regression discontinuity, and
    difference-in-differences.
  </p>
  <p style="color:var(--ink-soft); max-width:42rem;">
    I am a Senior Consultant at Research &amp; Planning Consultants, LP. Before
    that I spent six years at RAND as an economist and taught microeconomics and
    cost-benefit analysis at the RAND School of Public Policy. I hold a
    Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Oklahoma.
  </p>

<div class="section-label">Featured</div>

```{=html}
<div class="paper-card" style="border-left:4px solid var(--clay);">
  <h3><a href="research/fences-and-fortunes/">Fences and Fortunes: The Effect of Enhanced Border Enforcement on El Paso</a></h3>
  <div class="meta">with Robin Grier and Kevin Grier · Under review</div>
  <p class="abstract">
    In 1993, Operation Hold the Line put a wall of Border Patrol agents between
    El Paso and Ciudad Juárez. Crossings collapsed — and so did incomes, house
    values, and business growth on the U.S. side. We estimate the operation's
    causal effects and find its costs to El Paso swamped its benefits.
  </p>

```
